claim: The mitochondrial calcium uniporter is a Ca2+-gated ion channel complex that controls mitochondrial Ca2+ entry and regulates cell metabolism.
source: The mitochondrial calcium uniporter is a Ca2+-gated ion channel complex that controls mitochondrial Ca2+ entry and regulates cell metabolism.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: MCU and EMRE form the channel of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter.
source: MCU and EMRE form the channel while Ca2+-dependent regulation is conferred by MICU1 and MICU2 through an enigmatic process.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction (Baughman et al., 2011; Chaudhuri et al., 2013; De Stefani et al., 2011; Kovács-Bogdán et al., 2014; Sancak et al., 2013).

claim: Ca2+-dependent regulation of the uniporter is conferred by MICU1 and MICU2.
source: MCU and EMRE form the channel while Ca2+-dependent regulation is conferred by MICU1 and MICU2 through an enigmatic process.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript (Csordás et al., 2013; Kamer et al., 2017; Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Patron et al., 2014; Patron et al., 2019; Payne et al., 2017; Perocchi et al., 2010; Plovanich et al., 2013).

claim: A cryo-EM structure of an MCU-EMRE-MICU1-MICU2 holocomplex was determined at 3.3 Å resolution.
source: We present a cryo-EM structure of an MCU-EMRE-MICU1-MICU2 holocomplex comprising MCU and EMRE subunits from the beetle Tribolium castaneum in complex with a human MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer at 3.3 Å resolution.
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: A uniporter interaction domain on MICU1 binds to a channel receptor site comprising MCU and EMRE subunits to inhibit ion flow under resting Ca2+ conditions.
source: With analogy to how neuronal channels are blocked by protein toxins, a uniporter interaction domain on MICU1 binds to a channel receptor site comprising MCU and EMRE subunits to inhibit ion flow under resting Ca2+ conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figures 2 and 3, and functional data in Figure 3E.

claim: A Ca2+-bound structure of MICU1-MICU2 was determined at 3.1 Å resolution.
source: A Ca2+-bound structure of MICU1-MICU2 at 3.1 Å resolution indicates how Ca2+-dependent changes enable dynamic response to cytosolic Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The uniporter is one of the most selective Ca2+ channels known.
source: The uniporter is one of the most selective Ca2+ channels known and it is only activated once cytosolic Ca2+ levels reach a threshold (of approximately 0.4–3 μM) (Csordás et al., 2013; Kirichok et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2016; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012b; Payne et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The uniporter is only activated once cytosolic Ca2+ levels reach a threshold of approximately 0.4–3 μM.
source: The uniporter is one of the most selective Ca2+ channels known and it is only activated once cytosolic Ca2+ levels reach a threshold (of approximately 0.4–3 μM) (Csordás et al., 2013; Kirichok et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2016; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012b; Payne et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: MCU constitutes the pore of the uniporter through which Ca2+ ions flow.
source: The protein MCU constitutes the pore of the uniporter through which Ca2+ ions flow and EMRE, a small transmembrane protein that associates with MCU, is necessary for Ca2+ uptake in metazoan organisms (Baughman et al., 2011; Chaudhuri et al., 2013; De Stefani et al., 2011; Kovács-Bogdán et al., 2014; Sancak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: EMRE is necessary for Ca2+ uptake in metazoan organisms.
source: The protein MCU constitutes the pore of the uniporter through which Ca2+ ions flow and EMRE, a small transmembrane protein that associates with MCU, is necessary for Ca2+ uptake in metazoan organisms (Baughman et al., 2011; Chaudhuri et al., 2013; De Stefani et al., 2011; Kovács-Bogdán et al., 2014; Sancak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers reside in the intermembrane space (IMS).
source: Studies have resolved that MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers reside in the intermembrane space (IMS) where they regulate the uniporter by responding to [Ca2+]IMS (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Patron et al., 2014; Plovanich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers regulate the uniporter by responding to [Ca2+]IMS.
source: Studies have resolved that MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers reside in the intermembrane space (IMS) where they regulate the uniporter by responding to [Ca2+]IMS (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Patron et al., 2014; Plovanich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: [Ca2+]IMS closely follows the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration due to the permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: [Ca2+]IMS, which closely follows the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration due to the permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane, is sensed by EF-hand motifs in each protein.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial membrane permeability.

claim: [Ca2+]IMS is sensed by EF-hand motifs in MICU1 and MICU2.
source: [Ca2+]IMS, which closely follows the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration due to the permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane, is sensed by EF-hand motifs in each protein.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing EF-hand domains in MICU1 and MICU2 (Figure 4).

claim: At resting cytosolic [Ca2+] (~100 nM), MICU1-MICU2 and MICU1-MICU3 heterodimers prevent ion conduction through the channel.
source: At the ~100 nM resting level of [Ca2+]cytosol, MICU1-MICU2 and MICU1-MICU3 heterodimers prevent ion conduction through the channel, and they permit it when Ca2+ levels rise (Csordás et al., 2013; Kamer et al., 2017; Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Liu et al., 2016; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012b; Paillard et al., 2017; Patron et al., 2014; Patron et al., 2019; Payne et al., 2017; Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 and MICU1-MICU3 heterodimers permit ion conduction when Ca2+ levels rise.
source: At the ~100 nM resting level of [Ca2+]cytosol, MICU1-MICU2 and MICU1-MICU3 heterodimers prevent ion conduction through the channel, and they permit it when Ca2+ levels rise (Csordás et al., 2013; Kamer et al., 2017; Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Liu et al., 2016; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012b; Paillard et al., 2017; Patron et al., 2014; Patron et al., 2019; Payne et al., 2017; Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The amino acids facing the IMS are identical between human and beetle MCU/EMRE.
source: The amino acids facing the IMS, where MICU1-MICU2 resides, are identical between human and beetle MCU/EMRE and adopt analogous conformations in structures of the human and beetle channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and structural comparison in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cardiolipin is important for the function of the uniporter.
source: Cardiolipin was included because we recently identified that this lipid is important for the function of the uniporter (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The NTD of metazoan MCU is dispensable for mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake.
source: Because the NTD is dispensable for mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Baradaran et al., 2018; Oxenoid et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019), we removed this domain for high-resolution structural studies.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TcMCUΔNTD and TcEMRE coexpressed catalyze Ca2+ uptake into human mitochondria.
source: We have recently shown that the TcMCU and TcEMRE constructs used for structural analysis (TcMCUΔNTD and TcEMRE coexpressed) catalytze Ca2+ uptake into human mitochondria (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A disulfide bond formed between flexible C-terminal regions of MICU1 and MICU2 helps stabilize the heterodimer in cells.
source: In cells, a disulfide bond formed between flexible C-terminal regions of MICU1 and MICU2 helps stabilize the heterodimer (Kamer et al., 2019; Patron et al., 2014; Petrungaro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Most channels were associated with one MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer in the cryo-EM data.
source: From a large dataset containing approximately 17 million particle images, single particle analysis indicated that most channels were associated with one MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data analysis shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Two MICU1-MICU2 complexes were observed in approximately 2% of channel assemblies.
source: Two MICU1-MICU2 complexes were observed in approximately 2% of channel assemblies (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, as assessed from 2D class averages of side views).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data analysis shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 associate as a heterodimer and bind to the surface of the channel at the IMS entrance of its pore.
source: MICU1 and MICU2 associate as a heterodimer and bind to the surface of the channel at the IMS entrance of its pore (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Interactions with the channel are mediated solely by MICU1; MICU2 makes no visible contacts with MCU or EMRE.
source: Interactions with the channel are mediated solely by MICU1; MICU2 makes no visible contacts with MCU or EMRE.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The conformation of the pore is indistinguishable from that observed in a cryo-EM structure of TcMCU-EMRE without MICU1-MICU2.
source: The conformation of the pore is indistinguishable from that observed in a cryo-EM structure of TcMCU-EMRE without MICU1-MICU2 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Wang et al., 2020), which suggests that unlike gating conformational changes in many other ion channels, control by MICU1-MICU2 is not accomplished through motions of pore-lining helices.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control by MICU1-MICU2 is not accomplished through motions of pore-lining helices.
source: The conformation of the pore is indistinguishable from that observed in a cryo-EM structure of TcMCU-EMRE without MICU1-MICU2 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Wang et al., 2020), which suggests that unlike gating conformational changes in many other ion channels, control by MICU1-MICU2 is not accomplished through motions of pore-lining helices.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison showing no change in pore conformation.

claim: The ion-selectivity filter is formed by a fourfold assembly of the WDXXEP signature sequences of MCU subunits.
source: The structure of the holocomplex provides the most well-defined density to date for the ion-selectivity filter, which is formed by a fourfold assembly of the WDXXEP signature sequences of MCU subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E.

claim: The 'D' and 'E' residues of the WDXXEP motif (Asp 261 and Glu 264) form two rings of acidic amino acids that line the pore of the channel.
source: The 'D' and 'E' residues of this motif (Asp 261 and Glu 264) form two rings of acidic amino acids that line the pore of the channel and can coordinate Ca2+ through water-mediated ('D' ring) or direct interactions ('E' ring) (Baradaran et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019; Yoo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and structural data.

claim: Strong density assigned as Ca2+ is present within the 'E' ring under conditions of <1 nM Ca2+.
source: Strong density that we assign as Ca2+ on the basis of its coordination and analogy to other structures of MCU is present within the 'E' ring (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E.

claim: The Ca2+ site in the 'E' ring is the high-affinity (Kd ≤2 nM) Ca2+ binding site previously postulated from electrical recordings.
source: Its presence under conditions of <1 nM Ca2+ identifies this site as the high-affinity (Kd ≤2 nM) Ca2+ binding site previously postulated from electrical recordings made from mitoplasts that is thought to contribute to the channel's high selectivity for Ca2+ (Kirichok et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation and supported by a citation.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 binding does not displace Ca2+ from the 'E' ring site.
source: MICU1-MICU2 binding does not displace Ca2+ from this site.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing Ca2+ present in the 'E' ring in the holocomplex structure.

claim: Three EMRE subunits are observed at the periphery of the TMD (EMRE 1–3).
source: Three EMRE subunits are observed at the periphery of the TMD (EMRE 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Density for a fourth EMRE subunit is conspicuously absent.
source: Density for a fourth, like that observed in structures without MICU1-MICU2 (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019), is conspicuously absent (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: MICU1 interacts with only EMRE 1, which has the most well-defined density.
source: MICU1 interacts with only EMRE 1, which has the most well-defined density (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 5D.

claim: MICU1 contains three domains: an N-lobe, a C-lobe, and an N-terminal domain (UID).
source: MICU1 contains three domains (Wang et al., 2014): an N-lobe and a C-lobe, which contain its Ca2+-binding sites, and an N-terminal domain, which we name the uniporter interaction domain (UID) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3A and a citation.

claim: The UID mediates all observed interactions with the channel.
source: The UID mediates all observed interactions with the channel.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The UID comprises three α-helices (α1, α2, α3) and a small β-sheet formed by strands β1, β2 and β3.
source: The UID comprises three α-helices (α1, α2, α3) and a small β-sheet formed by strands β1, β2 and β3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Residues on α1 and α2 and a tight turn connecting these helices at Pro 124 directly contact the IMS surface of the channel.
source: Residues on α1 and α2 and a tight turn connecting these helices at Pro 124 directly contact the IMS surface of the channel (Figure 3D,F–G).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3D, F, and G.

claim: The receptor site for MICU1 on the channel is relatively flat and spans three MCU subunits and one EMRE subunit.
source: The receptor is relatively flat and spans three MCU subunits and one EMRE subunit.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The amino acids comprising the receptor site are conserved among metazoan channels and are identical between human and beetle channels.
source: The amino acids comprising it (MCU residues: Trp 255B, Tyr 258A&B, Ser 259B, Asp 261A,B&D, and Ile 262A&B, and EMRE residue Leu 92, Figure 3C) are conserved among metazoan channels and are identical between human and beetle channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B and structural comparison in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conformation of the receptor site is indistinguishable from the unliganded conformations of both beetle and human MCU-EMRE complexes.
source: Apart from the absence of EMRE 4, the conformation of the receptor site is indistinguishable from the unliganded conformations of both beetle and human MCU-EMRE complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The interacting residues on α1 (Phe 106, Arg 107, Lys 110, Val 111, Tyr 114, Arg 117, and Tyr 121) are identical in beetle MICU1 and conserved among animals.
source: The interacting residues on α1 (Phe 106, Arg 107, Lys 110, Val 111, Tyr 114, Arg 117, and Tyr 121) are identical in beetle MICU1 and conserved among animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A hydrophobic interaction between Phe 106 of α1 and Leu 92 of EMRE comprises the only contact observed between MICU1 and EMRE.
source: A hydrophobic interaction between Phe 106 of α1 and the IMS end of EMRE's transmembrane helix at Leu 92, which is also highly conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), comprises the only contact observed between MICU1 and EMRE (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The mouth of the pore is coordinated by Lys 126 and Arg 129 from α2, and Ser 122 of the α1-α2 turn through a network of hydrogen bonds that involves three of the four MCU-Asp 261 residues of the 'D' ring.
source: The mouth of the pore is coordinated by Lys 126 and Arg 129 from α2, and Ser 122 of the α1-α2 turn through a network of hydrogen bonds that involves three of the four MCU-Asp 261 residues of the 'D' ring (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: The 'D' ring is involved in MICU1 binding.
source: This confirms the previous hypothesis that the 'D' ring is involved in MICU1 binding (Paillard et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and citations to previous hypotheses.

claim: The MICU1 residues participating in the hydrogen-bonding network (Tyr 114, Ser 122, Asp 125, Lys 126, Arg 129, and Asp 169) are conserved.
source: The MICU1 residues participating in the hydrogen-bonding network (Tyr 114, Ser 122, Asp 125, Lys 126, Arg 129, and Asp 169) are conserved (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), but none were previously predicted to mediate interactions with the channel (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Robust mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake was observed when wild type MICU1 was expressed.
source: As expected, robust mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake was observed when wild type MICU1 was expressed and uptake was suppressed by mutations within the Ca2+-binding EF-hands of MICU1 that cause it to constitutively inhibit the channel (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 5; Kamer and Mootha, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Uptake was suppressed by mutations within the Ca2+-binding EF-hands of MICU1 that cause it to constitutively inhibit the channel.
source: As expected, robust mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake was observed when wild type MICU1 was expressed and uptake was suppressed by mutations within the Ca2+-binding EF-hands of MICU1 that cause it to constitutively inhibit the channel (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 5; Kamer and Mootha, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 5, and a citation.

claim: Residues that interact with MCU or EMRE relieve inhibition when mutated to alanine.
source: Residues that were observed to interact with MCU or EMRE relieve this inhibition when mutated to alanine.
evidence: This is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A single K126A mutation essentially eliminates inhibition by MICU1.
source: Lys 126 seems particularly crucial – a single K126A mutation essentially eliminates inhibition by MICU1.
evidence: This is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The regions of the UID that interact with the channel are absent in MICU2 or MICU3.
source: The regions of the UID that interact with the channel are absent in MICU2 or MICU3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The α1 helix, the conserved Pro 124 in the bend between α1 and α2, and residues that interact with the 'D' ring are unique to MICU1.
source: The α1 helix, the conserved Pro 124 in the bend between α1 and α2, and residues that interact with the 'D' ring are unique to MICU1.
evidence: This is supported by structural and sequence comparison data.

claim: The uniqueness of the UID to MICU1 explains why MICU1 is distinct from MICU2 and MICU3 in its ability to interact with MCU/EMRE.
source: This explains why MICU1 is distinct from MICU2 and MICU3 in its ability to interact with MCU/EMRE, and it explains the observation that MICU2 and MICU3 have non-redundant roles in comparison to MICU1 in the regulation of the channel (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Patron et al., 2014; Patron et al., 2019; Payne et al., 2017; Xing et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by citations.

claim: The interaction with the pore is reminiscent of the interaction between μ-conotoxin KIIIA and the Nav1.2 channel.
source: The interaction with the pore is reminiscent of the interaction between μ-conotoxin KIIIA, a small pore-blocking peptide toxin found in the venom of a cone snail, with the extracellular surface of the neuronal Nav1.2 channel (Pan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2007; Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is an analogy drawn from structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6 and supported by citations.

claim: A short α-helical region of μ-conotoxin KIIIA lies horizontally at the entrance of the pore of Nav1.2, in a similar manner to the binding of the α2 helix of MICU1 with the uniporter.
source: A short α-helical region of the toxin lies horizontally at the entrance of the pore of Nav1.2, in a similar manner to the binding of the α2 helix of MICU1 with the uniporter.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn from structural comparison.

claim: An arginine and a lysine residue separated by one turn of the toxin's α-helix coordinate acidic amino acids at the entrance of the selectivity filter in Nav1.2.
source: As in the UID-uniporter interface, an arginine and a lysine residue that are separated by one turn of the toxin's α-helix coordinate acidic amino acids at the entrance of the selectivity filter (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: μ-conotoxin KIIIA blocks approximately 90% of Na+ current though the Nav1.2 channel.
source: The binding of the toxin is slightly off-center such that two of four analogous acidic amino acids are coordinated and the pore is not completely occluded – nevertheless this toxin blocks approximately 90% of Na+ current though the channel (Zhang et al., 2007; Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The UID interacts with three of the four 'D'-ring amino acids at the mouth of the uniporter's pore.
source: The UID interacts with three of the four 'D'-ring amino acids at the mouth of the uniporter's pore and the occlusion of the pore is more extensive than observed for Nav1.2 by μ-conotoxin KIIIA (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figures 2, 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The occlusion of the pore by the UID is more extensive than observed for Nav1.2 by μ-conotoxin KIIIA.
source: The UID interacts with three of the four 'D'-ring amino acids at the mouth of the uniporter's pore and the occlusion of the pore is more extensive than observed for Nav1.2 by μ-conotoxin KIIIA (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figures 2, 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: MICU1 binding inhibits the flow of Ca2+ ions by both obstructing the IMS entrance of the pore and by shielding the negative charge of the 'D' ring through coordination with basic amino acids.
source: The structure of the holocomplex and its similarity to a pore-blocking toxin complex indicate that MICU1 binding inhibits the flow of Ca2+ ions by both obstructing the IMS entrance of the pore and by shielding the negative charge of the 'D' ring through coordination with basic amino acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and analogy to toxin-channel interactions.

claim: The MICU1-MICU2 portion of the holocomplex is roughly parallelogram shaped, with overall dimensions of approximately 70 × 65 × 35 Å, under resting conditions.
source: The MICU1-MICU2 portion of the holocomplex is roughly parallelogram shaped, with overall dimensions of approximately 70 × 65 × 35 Å, under resting conditions in which its EF-hand domains are in Ca2+-free apo states (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: One of the large relatively-flat surfaces of MICU1-MICU2 faces and curves slightly toward the membrane due to a slight bend between MICU1 and MICU2.
source: One of its large relatively-flat surfaces faces and curves slightly toward the membrane due to a slight bend between MICU1 and MICU2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer has pseudo twofold symmetry and two analogous interfaces between the subunits.
source: The heterodimer has pseudo twofold symmetry and two analogous interfaces between the subunits (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: Hydrophobic amino acids predominate the interfaces between MICU1 and MICU2.
source: Hydrophobic amino acids predominate the interfaces, with MICU1-Met 229, MICU1-Phe 383, MICU2-Met 183, and MICU2-Met 337 making analogous and particularly extensive contacts within them (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The interfacial residues between MICU1 and MICU2 are conserved in MICU3.
source: The interfacial residues are conserved in MICU3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which suggests that the neuron-specific MICU1-MICU3 heterodimer has a similar arrangement.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: All four Ca2+-binding EF-hand motifs of the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer are in the apo state under resting [Ca2+] conditions.
source: As would be expected under resting [Ca2+] conditions, all four Ca2+-binding EF-hand motifs of the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer ('EF1' and 'EF4' of both subunits) are in the apo state and the heterodimer is superimposable with a previous apo structure of MICU1-MICU2 alone (Park et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 6, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, and a citation.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 has an affinity for cardiolipin.
source: From biochemical analysis of the purified protein, and in acoord with a previous report that MICU1-MICU2 has an affinity for cardiolipin (Kamer et al., 2017), we found that the heterodimer associates with lipid membranes and lipid nanodiscs that contain cardiolipin (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and Figure 4F, and a citation.

claim: The association of MICU1-MICU2 with lipid membranes is independent of Ca2+.
source: This association is independent of Ca2+ - both Ca2+-free and Ca2+-bound heterodimers bind to liposomes.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Ca2+ binding makes the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer more compact and markedly more bent between MICU1 and MICU2.
source: The structure reveals a substantial conformational change upon Ca2+ binding that makes the heterodimer more compact and markedly more bent between MICU1 and MICU2 (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Ca2+ dependent rearrangements of the EF-hand motifs produce the bend in MICU1-MICU2.
source: Ca2+ dependent rearrangements of the EF-hand motifs that involve their helix turn helix elements produce this bend (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ca2+ binding induces a rotation of the UID relative to MICU1.
source: Ca2+ binding also induces a rotation of the UID relative to MICU1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The side of the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer that associates with the nanodisc is the same as the one that faces the channel.
source: The side of the heterodimer that associates with the nanodisc is the same as the one that faces the channel (Figures 1A and 4F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figures 1A and 4F.

claim: The bending motion of MICU1-MICU2 acts like a lever against the membrane to pry MICU1 from the mouth of the pore when [Ca2+]IMS is elevated.
source: Rather than inserting into the membrane, we hypothesize that the bending motion of MICU1-MICU2 acts like a lever against the membrane to pry MICU1 from the mouth of the pore when [Ca2+]IMS is elevated.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural data and thermodynamic considerations.

claim: The Ca2+-dependent conformational changes within MICU1 cause a rotation of the UID that could disfavor binding to the channel.
source: Additionally, the Ca2+-dependent conformational changes within MICU1 cause a rotation of the UID that could disfavor binding to the channel (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The conformational changes would dislodge the UID from the blocking conformation, allowing Ca2+ ions to permeate though the channel while [Ca2+]IMS remains elevated.
source: The conformational changes would dislodge the UID from the blocking conformation, which would allow Ca2+ ions to permeate though the channel while [Ca2+]IMS remains elevated.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and the proposed mechanism.

claim: When resting [Ca2+]IMS is restored, a MICU1-MICU2 complex, again devoid of its Ca2+ ligands, would resume the blocking configuration.
source: When resting [Ca2+]IMS is restored, a MICU1-MICU2 complex, again devoid of its Ca2+ ligands, would resume the blocking configuration (Figure 5, left, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanism and structural data.

claim: The mechanism of MICU1-MICU2 control is compatible with the observed dimerization of human MCU-EMRE channels due to association of their NTDs.
source: This mechanism of MICU1-MICU2 control is compatible with the observed dimerization of human MCU-EMRE channels that is due to association of their NTDs – there is sufficient room for MICU1-MICU2 complexes to associate with both channels of the dimer and to control Ca2+ influx through their pores (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: During the preparation of this manuscript, cryo-EM structures of a holocomplex comprising human MCU, EMRE, MICU1 and MICU2 subunits in resting and activated [Ca2+] conditions were reported.
source: During the preparation of this manuscript, cryo-EM structures of a holocomplex comprising human MCU, EMRE, MICU1 and MICU2 subunits in resting and activated [Ca2+] conditions were reported (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about concurrent work, supported by a citation.

claim: The conclusions of the concurrent work are congruous with the present study and validate the proposed mechanism of Ca2+-dependent regulation of the uniporter by MICU1-MICU2.
source: The conclusions of that work are congruous with the present study and validate the proposed mechanism of Ca2+-dependent regulation of the uniporter by MICU1-MICU2.
evidence: This is a comparison with concurrent work, supported by a citation.

claim: An additional interaction with the 'D'-ring at the mouth of the pore, involving a loop region of MICU1 (amino acids 258–274), was observed in the concurrent work.
source: Interestingly, an additional interaction with the 'D'-ring at the mouth of the pore, involving a loop region of MICU1 (amino acids 258–274) that is disordered in our structure, was observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a comparison with concurrent work, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: A structure of an intact holocomplex at elevated levels of [Ca2+] indicates that the Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 regulatory complex binds adjacent to the pore.
source: A structure of an intact holocomplex at elevated levels of [Ca2+], which was included in the recent work, indicates that the Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 regulatory complex binds adjacent to the pore in essentially the same manner that we propose (Figure 5, right, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a comparison with concurrent work, supported by Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mechanism of Ca2+-dependent control of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter by MICU1-MICU2 is distinct from conformational changes that underlie gating in many other ion channels.
source: This work reveals a mechanism for Ca2+-dependent control of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter by the MICU1-MICU2 regulatory complex. The mechanism is distinct from the conformational changes that underlie gating, the process by which ion channels permit or prevent ion condution, in many other ion channels – these often involve changes in the dimensions of their ion conduction pores due to motions of transmembrane α-helices that line these pores, as was first exemplified by structural studies of potassium channels (MacKinnon, 2003).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data and comparison with other ion channels, supported by a citation.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers operate like endogenous pore-blocking toxins, the binding of which is governed by Ca2+-dependent conformational changes within them.
source: MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers, and by analogy MICU1-MICU3 heterodimers in neurons, thus confer Ca2+-dependent gating to the uniporter by operating like endogenous pore-blocking toxins, the binding of which is governed by Ca2+-dependent conformational changes within them.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data and analogy to toxin-channel interactions.

claim: A single MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer appears capable of conferring Ca2+-dependent control properties to the channel.
source: A single MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer appears capable of conferring these properties for the simple reason that the receptor site on the channel can accommodate only one UID.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing the receptor site.

claim: More than one MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer may be tethered to the channel at any given time.
source: However, more than one MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer may be tethered to the channel at any given time, as is indicated by the cryo-EM analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data showing a small fraction of particles with two MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers.

claim: Nucleation of more than one heterodimer in the vicinity of the channel would increase the local concentration of MICU1-MICU2 and facilitate a rapid response following restoration of resting cytosolic Ca2+ levels.
source: Nucleation of more than one heterodimer in the vicinity of the channel would increase the local concentration of MICU1-MICU2 and facilitate a rapid response following restoration of resting cytosolic Ca2+ levels.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observations.

claim: The displacement of an EMRE subunit (EMRE 4) from the TMD might serve as an additional mechanism to control ion flow.
source: While MICU1-MICU2 visibly interacts with only one EMRE subunit, the displacement of an EMRE subunit (EMRE 4) from the TMD might serve as an additional mechanism to control ion flow since the expression of EMRE is necessary for Ca2+ uptake by mitochondria (Liu et al., 2016; Sancak et al., 2013; Tsai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observation and supported by citations.

claim: The displacement of an EMRE subunit suggests that the number of EMRE subunits associated with an MCU tetramer can vary.
source: Additionally, the displacement of an EMRE subunit suggests that the number of EMRE subunits associated with an MCU tetramer can vary, as has been inferred from a recent study (Payne et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation and supported by a citation.
